notions.question: Why do some English words seem to "disappear" in speech?
notions.definition: English is a stress-timed language: content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) are stressed, while function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns, conjunctions) are usually pronounced in their weak form, with the vowel reduced to schwa /ə/. Thus "to" is pronounced /tə/, "for" /fə/, "and" /ən/ or /n/, "can" /kən/, "was" /wəz/, "of" /əv/. Spotting these reduced forms helps you understand real spoken English; producing them makes your English sound more natural. The strong form reappears at the end of a sentence or under emphasis (What are you looking for? — /fɔː/).

lignes: I want to go /aɪ wɒnt tə ɡəʊ/

termes.definition: Reduced pronunciation of a function word.
Reduced central vowel, the most frequent vowel in English.
Prominence given to content words.

exemple.texte: "We'd like to order two hundred units" is pronounced roughly /wiːd laɪk tə ˈɔːdə tuː ˈhʌndrəd ˈjuːnɪts/: only like, order, two, hundred and units are stressed.

confusions.explication: The difference between affirmative and negative is heard mainly through stress and vowel quality.

verification: Which words are stressed in "I'm going to the bank to get some cash"?

notions.question: Why do words run together to the point of becoming unrecognisable?
notions.definition: In spoken English, words run together: a final consonant links to the following vowel (linking: turn_off → /tɜːnɒf/); in British English a linking /r/ appears between two vowels (far_away → /fɑːrəweɪ/); sounds change on contact with each other (assimilation: did you → /dɪdʒuː/, would you → /wʊdʒuː/, don't you → /dəʊntʃuː/, ten pounds → /tem paʊndz/) or disappear (elision: next day → /neks deɪ/, kind of → /kaɪnə/). The informal forms gonna (going to), wanna (want to) and gotta (got to) are examples of this: you need to recognise them but avoid them in professional writing.

termes.definition: The joining of words in speech.
Change in a sound under the influence of a neighbouring sound.
Loss of a sound.

exemple.texte: "What do you want to do?" is often pronounced /wɒdʒə wɒnə duː/: without knowing these phenomena, you would not recognise a single word.

confusions.explication: These are forms of informal speech and must be avoided in professional writing.

verification: How is "would you" often pronounced in everyday English?

notions.question: How can you understand speakers with very different accents?
notions.definition: English has a wide variety of accents: British (including Received Pronunciation and the regional accents of Scotland, the North and London), Irish, American (General American, Southern accents), Canadian and Australian, as well as the English of non-native speakers (India, Africa, Europe, Asia), who are the majority in international business exchanges. Some common differences: pronunciation of /r/ after a vowel (rhotic in the United States, generally not in standard British English: car), the vowel in "bath, dance" (/ɑː/ UK, /æ/ US), the American flapped "t" (water → /ˈwɑːɾər/). Regular exposure to a variety of accents is the best preparation.

termes.definition: Way of pronouncing specific to a region or group.
Reference British accent.
English used between non-native speakers.

exemple.texte: During a video conference with an Indian buyer, a Scottish supplier and a Dutch freight forwarder, the export assistant restates the decisions in writing to make sure everyone has understood the same deadlines.

confusions.explication: A strong accent does not indicate a poor command of English.

verification: Name two differences in pronunciation between British and American English.

flashcards.question: Explain why spoken English is hard to understand: weak forms, linking, accents.
flashcards.reponse: Stress-timed language: content words are stressed, function words are reduced (to /tə/, for /fə/, and /ən/, can /kən/, of /əv/). Connected speech: linking (pick it up), British linking R, assimilation (did you /dɪdʒuː/), elision (last week), informal forms (gonna, wanna). Varied accents: British, American (rhotic, flapped t, schedule with /sk/), international English of non-native speakers. Expose yourself to them regularly.
erreurs: Writing gonna in a professional document

notions.question: How do you understand an audio or video document in English during an exam?
notions.definition: Listening comprehension works in stages. Before listening: read the instructions and the title, predict the topic and the likely vocabulary. First, global listening: identify the situation (who is speaking, to whom, where, why), the type of document (interview, news bulletin, lecture), the general topic and the tone. Following, focused listenings: pick out specific information (figures, names, dates, causes, consequences, opinions), relying on stressed words, cognates and connectors (but, however, so, because). You accept that you will not understand everything: you rebuild the meaning from the elements you have identified and from the context.

etapes: Rebuild the meaning and check that it is coherent

termes.definition: Ability to understand a sound document.
Word that is similar in both languages.
Hypotheses about the content made before listening.

exemple.texte: Document: radio interview with the director of a British port. Listening 1: the topic is the consequences of Brexit on traffic. Listening 2: three ideas (longer checks, investment, new services). Listening 3: figures (waiting time up from 20 minutes to 2 hours, 50 million pounds invested).

confusions.b: Understanding the gist and the details required
confusions.explication: The goal is meaning, not a full transcription.

verification: What should you identify during the first listening?

notions.question: How do you quickly note down the essentials of an oral document?
notions.definition: Effective note-taking does not try to write everything down: it captures key ideas, figures and logical links, using abbreviations and symbols (↑ increase, ↓ decrease, → consequence, ≠ contrast, = equal, + addition, ∵ because), keywords rather than sentences, and an uncluttered layout (columns: topic / ideas / details; or a mind map). You can take notes in English to save time, then rephrase in French if the restitution requires it. Figures and proper nouns are noted immediately.

termes.definition: Technique for noting down the essentials quickly.
Tree-like representation of ideas.

exemple.texte: "Port traffic ↓ 15% since 2021 b/c customs checks → waiting time 20 min → 2 h. Govt + port invest £50m (new lanes). Manager: optimistic, 2027."

confusions.explication: Writing full sentences makes you miss the rest of the document.

verification: Suggest five useful symbols for note-taking.

notions.question: How do you report on an oral document clearly and faithfully?
notions.definition: The report renders, in French or in English depending on the instructions, the content of an oral document: a presentation of the document (type, source, speakers, topic), then the main ideas in a logical order (not necessarily that of the document), with the significant details (figures, examples); where relevant, the speakers' points of view (attributed: "according to the director…"). It is objective, written in full sentences with connectors, and respects the required length. You only report what you have understood and heard, without inventing anything.

etapes: Introductory sentence: type of document, source, speakers, topic
Points of view attributed to their authors

termes.definition: Faithful rendering of a document.
Person who is speaking.

exemple.texte: "This document is an excerpt from an interview broadcast by a British radio station, in which the director of the port of Dover discusses the consequences of Brexit. She explains that traffic has fallen by 15% since 2021 because of customs checks…"

confusions.explication: The report stays faithful to the document; a personal opinion is given only if the instructions ask for it.

verification: What should the first sentence of a report contain?

questions.enonce: What should you do before the first listening?

choix.texte: Read the instructions and predict the topic and vocabulary
Write down everything you will hear

questions.enonce: True or false: in a report, you may fill in passages you did not understand with your own knowledge, without saying so.

choix.explication: You only report what the document says.
Inventing content is a failure of faithfulness.

flashcards.question: Describe the complete method for listening comprehension: listening, note-taking, report.
flashcards.reponse: Listening: predict (instructions, title, vocabulary), global listening (situation, speakers, topic, tone), focused listenings (ideas, figures, names, opinions), rebuilding the meaning. Notes: keywords, symbols (↑ ↓ → ≠), abbreviations, figures noted at once, column layout. Report: presentation of the document, main ideas in order, details, attributed points of view, full sentences, objectivity, required length respected.

notions.titre: Giving an oral presentation in English
notions.question: How do you structure and deliver a successful professional presentation in English?
notions.definition: An effective oral presentation is structured and marked out by transition expressions (signposting). Introduction: greet the audience, introduce yourself, announce the topic, the objective and the outline ("Today I'd like to talk about… First… Then… Finally…"). Main body: one idea per part, explicit transitions ("Let's move on to…", "This brings me to…"), commentary on visuals ("As you can see on this slide…", "This chart shows…"). Conclusion: summary, recommendation, thanks and an invitation to ask questions ("To sum up…", "Thank you for your attention. I'd be happy to answer any questions."). You speak from notes, without reading, articulating clearly and looking at the audience.

lignes: Good morning, everyone. My name is… and I'm in charge of…
The purpose of this presentation is to… I've divided it into three parts.
Let's now turn to… / Moving on to…
As you can see, sales have risen steadily since 2023.
To sum up, … I'd recommend that we…
I'd be happy to take any questions.

termes.definition: Expressions that guide the audience.
One page of projected presentation material.
Projected chart, table or image.

exemple.texte: "Good afternoon. Today I'd like to present the results of our market study on Mexico. First, I'll give you an overview of the market; then I'll look at the competition; finally, I'll make some recommendations."

confusions.explication: Slides support the talk; they do not replace it.

verification: Give three transition expressions in English.

notions.question: How do you take part effectively in a meeting, a call or a negotiation in English?
notions.definition: Spoken interaction requires knowing how to take and give the floor, give your opinion and qualify it, express agreement or disagreement tactfully, ask for clarification, rephrase to check understanding, and buy time to think. Softening expressions are essential in professional English ("I see your point, but…", "I'm not sure I agree", "Could you clarify what you mean by…?"). On the phone or in a video conference, you spell out names (international phonetic alphabet: Alpha, Bravo…), confirm figures and summarise in writing.

lignes: In my view… / I think we should…
I completely agree. / That's a good point.
I see what you mean, but… / I'm afraid I don't quite agree.
Could you clarify…? / What exactly do you mean by…?
So, if I understand correctly, you're saying that…
That's an interesting question. Let me think about it.

termes.en: to take the floor / to chip in
termes.definition: To speak up in a discussion.
To say something in other words to check understanding.
To say the letters of a word one by one.

exemple.texte: "I see your point about the delivery time, but I'm afraid we can't commit to two weeks. Could we agree on three weeks, with a penalty clause if we're late?"

confusions.explication: "I'm afraid we can't" = « Malheureusement, nous ne pouvons pas » ("Unfortunately, we cannot"), not a statement of fear.

verification: How do you politely express disagreement in a meeting?

questions.enonce: Which expression is used to move from one part of a presentation to the next?

choix.texte: "Let's move on to the next point."

questions.enonce: Which French sentence correctly renders "I'm afraid we can't accept this price"?

choix.texte: « Malheureusement, nous ne pouvons pas accepter ce prix. »
choix.explication: A softening formula ("Unfortunately, we cannot accept this price").
Mistranslation: "I'm afraid" does not express fear here.

choix.texte: « Nous acceptons ce prix avec crainte. »
choix.explication: Mistranslation: the sentence is a refusal, not a reluctant acceptance.
It is a refusal, not hesitation.

questions.enonce: Which expressions allow you to check understanding?

choix.texte: "So, if I understand correctly, you need delivery by May?"
"Could you clarify what you mean by 'flexible terms'?"

flashcards.question: Give the structure of an oral presentation in English and some expressions for interacting in a meeting.
flashcards.reponse: Presentation: opening (Good morning… My name is…), objective and outline (The purpose of this presentation is… First… Then… Finally…), transitions (Let's move on to…), visuals (As you can see…), conclusion (To sum up…), questions (I'd be happy to take any questions). Interaction: opinion (In my view…), agreement (That's a good point), polite disagreement (I see what you mean, but…), clarification (Could you clarify…?), rephrasing (So, if I understand correctly…), interrupting (Sorry to interrupt…).

synthese.titre: English comprehension and expression: the essentials
synthese.essentiel: Spoken English is hard to follow because it is stress-timed: content words are stressed, function words shrink to schwa, words run together and accents vary. The exam method is always the same: predict, listen globally then in detail, take notes with symbols, then write a faithful, structured report. In speaking, structure everything with signposting and soften opinions and disagreement.

chapitres.idee: Real spoken English reduces, links and varies its sounds: to understand it you must expect weak forms, connected speech and different accents.
points: Stress-timed language: content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) stressed; function words reduced
Weak forms use schwa /ə/: to /tə/, for /fə/, and /ən/, can /kən/, of /əv/, was /wəz/
Strong form returns at the end of a sentence or under emphasis: What are you looking for? /fɔː/
Connected speech: linking (pick it up), linking R in UK (far away), assimilation (did you /dɪdʒuː/), elision (last week /lɑːs wiːk/)
gonna, wanna, gotta: recognise them, never write them in professional English
Accents: UK (RP, Scotland, North, London), Irish, US, Canadian, Australian, and non-native speakers, who are the majority in business
UK/US: US rhotic (car /kɑːr/), bath /ɑː/ UK vs /æ/ US, US flapped t (water), schedule /ʃ/ UK vs /sk/ US

distinctions.difference: Heard through stress and vowel quality; the final /t/ is often barely audible.
Assimilation changes a sound (did you → /dɪdʒuː/); elision drops a sound (next day → /neks deɪ/).
A strong accent does not mean a poor command of English.

chapitres.memo: Stress the meaning, squash the grammar: content words are loud, function words whisper in schwa.
